Are B2B sales cycles hard, and how can teams shorten them?

B2B sales cycles can last weeks or months, depending on the deal’s value, the number of stakeholders involved, and the buyer’s approval requirements. Longer cycles can slow pipeline velocity by keeping opportunities open and delaying deal close dates.
According to sales-cycle benchmarks published by Optifai, the median B2B SaaS sales cycle is 84 days. The company’s published benchmarks also show how deal size relates to buying-process length.
The following sales-cycle ranges are reported by annual contract value (ACV), representing the 25th to 75th percentiles:
Small and midsize business deals (under $15,000 ACV): 14–30 days. Smaller deals generally involve fewer stakeholders and approval requirements.
Mid-market deals ($15,000–$100,000 ACV): 30–90 days. Larger purchases may involve additional budget, security, and procurement approval.
Enterprise deals (over $100,000 ACV): 90–180 days or longer. Higher-value purchases often involve more extensive legal reviews, technical evaluations, and approval processes.

These figures describe B2B SaaS sales, not every B2B industry. They provide useful benchmarks, but revenue teams should compare their own sales cycles with companies that have similar customers, deal sizes, and purchasing requirements.
Price isn’t the only reason B2B deals take longer, though. Several other factors can slow down the buying process even when a prospect is genuinely interested:

More people are involved in the decision. A buyer might be sold on the product, but that doesn’t mean the deal is ready to close. Finance may need to approve the budget, IT may need to review integrations, legal may need to check the contract, and senior leadership may still want to sign off.

Buyers have more to evaluate. B2B purchases often affect multiple teams, workflows, and systems, so buyers typically need more information before they feel comfortable deciding. That can mean demos, technical reviews, internal discussions, vendor comparisons, and multiple rounds of questions.

Approval processes can move slowly. Even when the buyer wants to move forward, internal procurement rules can add extra steps. A deal can sit for days or weeks while teams wait for budget approval, contract review, purchase orders, or other internal sign-offs.

Follow-up can lose momentum. Long gaps between conversations give deals more time to cool off. If the rep misses a follow-up, doesn’t answer a question quickly, or fails to bring the right stakeholder into the conversation, the buying process can stretch even further.

The buyer’s priorities can change. A new project, budget cut, leadership change, or competing initiative can push an active deal further down the list. The longer the sales cycle runs, the more likely something will change internally before the purchase is approved.
How to Shorten B2B Sales Cycles

Not every delay is within the sales team’s control. But teams can speed things up by qualifying deals more carefully, involving the right people earlier, and making the buying process easier to navigate.
The following actions can reduce avoidable delays. Teams can also use these B2B sales tips when reviewing their qualification, outreach, and follow-up processes:

Reps should confirm there’s a real need, an available budget, a clear decision process, and enough urgency to move forward. That makes it easier to spend time on deals with a realistic chance of closing, instead of carrying weak opportunities through the sales pipeline for months.
2. Identify the full buying group upfront.

A deal can slow down quickly when a new decision-maker appears late in the process. Reps should find out who needs to approve the purchase, who’ll use the product, and who may have concerns so those conversations can happen earlier.
3. Ask about the approval process before the final stage.

Sales teams shouldn’t wait until the buyer says yes to learn that legal, finance, procurement, or IT still need to review the deal. Asking about these steps early gives both sides more time to prepare documents, answer questions, and avoid last-minute surprises.
4. Make the business case easy to share internally.

The person speaking with the sales team may still need to convince several other people. Clear pricing, ROI estimates, product information, implementation details, and relevant proof points help an internal champion explain the value of the purchase without building the case from scratch.
5. Keep every deal moving toward a clear next step.

Each conversation should end with a specific action, owner, and timeline. That could be scheduling a technical review, sending a proposal, bringing finance into the conversation, or confirming who needs to approve the contract next.
6. Use the right tools to manage follow-up and pipeline activity.
Sales teams can lose valuable time when reps have to jump between multiple systems to find notes, check deal activity, or remember who needs a follow-up.

Sales Hub brings lead management, deal activity, automation, and pipeline reporting into one workspace. Teams can automate tasks and follow-ups, monitor deal progression, and identify stages where opportunities stall instead of relying on reps to track every activity manually.
7. Look at where deals spend the most time.

Average sales-cycle length only tells part of the story. Teams should look at how long deals sit in each stage and identify places where deals repeatedly slow down, whether that’s qualification, demos, proposals, security reviews, or contract approval.
Once those patterns are clear, it’s easier to fix the steps that are creating avoidable delays.
The Biggest B2B Challenges for Revenue Teams

The biggest B2B challenges often share a common cause: information, responsibilities, and processes become disconnected as a business grows. Data silos create reporting gaps, inconsistent handoffs slow sales, and manual work makes it harder to serve customers consistently.

The following 10 challenges show where revenue teams can look for problems, how those problems affect performance, and how to address them. A connected CRM and tools such as Sales Hub can help teams track opportunities, coordinate responsibilities, and identify operational bottlenecks.

A data silo is a collection of information that sits inside one team, department, or system and isn’t easily accessible to the rest of the organization. Platform fragmentation often creates these silos: when tools are disconnected, the data inside each tool stays disconnected too.

That can leave revenue teams working with incomplete versions of the customer. For example, a sales rep might not see that a prospect recently downloaded a high-intent asset, while a service rep may not know about a conversation the customer had with sales before onboarding.

As a result, teams duplicate work, reps spend more time searching for context, and leaders make decisions based on reports that don’t reflect the full customer journey. Data silos can also make it harder to spot where revenue is being lost because no single team has the complete picture.
Here are a few warning signs that point to siloed data:
Teams maintain separate records for the same customers.
Employees regularly ask other departments for information they can’t access themselves.
Reports from different teams don’t match.
Customer activity in one system isn’t visible in another.
Reps spend time checking multiple tools before contacting a prospect or customer.
Important context disappears when an account moves from one team to another.
Because HubSpot’s products share HubSpot Smart CRM, teams can use connected customer records instead of maintaining separate databases for each department.

For example, when marketing captures engagement data in a contact record, authorized sales and service users can view that information if their permissions and data configuration allow it. Shared records can reduce duplicate work and give employees more relevant context when they contact prospects or customers.

According to MuleSoft’s 2026 Connectivity Benchmark Report, surveyed organizations managed an average of 957 applications, with only 27% integrated. The report draws on a survey of 1,050 IT leaders at enterprises with at least 1,000 employees across nine markets, conducted in October and November 2025.

When so many systems operate independently, teams may work with different versions of customer data and spend extra time manually connecting information. These gaps can delay decisions, complicate reporting, and make customer interactions less consistent.
More time spent switching between tools

The problem also tends to grow with the tech stack. Adding another tool may solve one team’s immediate need, but it can create another data source, workflow, or integration the organization must maintain.
Platform fragmentation may be an issue if:
Teams regularly export and import data between systems.
Sales, marketing, and service report different numbers for the same customer or account.
Employees need several tools to understand a customer’s history.
Important information gets lost during team handoffs.
Reporting requires manually combining data from multiple platforms.
Integrations frequently break or require ongoing maintenance.

Unclear attribution makes it hard to tell which marketing and sales activities actually influenced a deal. A prospect might first find the company through search, attend a webinar, click a nurture email, and later speak with sales. But if those touchpoints live in different systems, it can be hard to see what really contributed to the conversion.

That creates a problem for revenue teams because budget decisions start relying on partial information. Marketing may keep investing in channels that look successful on paper while undervaluing the ones that actually help move buyers through the funnel.
A few signs usually show up when attribution is unclear:
Different teams credit different channels for the same deal.
Marketing can track leads but not what happens after they enter the sales process.
Revenue reports rely heavily on first-touch or last-touch data.
Teams struggle to connect campaign activity with closed revenue.
Budget decisions are based on channel-level metrics instead of full-funnel performance.

Marketing Hub connects marketing activity with CRM data so teams can examine how emails, forms, landing pages, and campaigns contribute to customer journeys. Attribution reporting helps teams evaluate those interactions using different models, depending on their subscription and available data.

With deal revenue attribution reporting, eligible teams can assign credit to recorded interactions using models such as linear or time-decay attribution rather than relying only on first- or last-touch data. The results depend on the available CRM data, qualifying interactions, and attribution model.
Revenue teams can use those reports to evaluate which activities appear to contribute to closed deals without treating attribution as proof that a particular interaction caused the sale.

Unclear ROI happens when revenue teams can see what they’re spending but can’t clearly connect that spend to business results. For example, marketing may invest heavily in paid ads, events, and email campaigns but still struggle to tell which activities are actually contributing to pipeline and revenue.
Without that connection, it becomes harder to decide where to increase spend, where to cut back, and which programs are worth repeating.
ROI may be difficult to measure when:
Teams can report campaign engagement but not the revenue generated.
Marketing spend and revenue data live in separate systems.
Leaders struggle to compare campaign costs with the value of resulting deals.
Budget decisions rely heavily on clicks, leads, or other activity metrics.
Teams can’t confidently explain which marketing investments are producing returns.

Marketing Hub provides campaign ROI reporting and, in eligible subscriptions, deal revenue attribution reporting. Campaign ROI reports compare recorded spending with revenue, attributed revenue, or associated deal value, depending on the account’s settings and subscription. Deal revenue attribution reports help teams examine which recorded marketing interactions received credit for closed revenue under a selected attribution model.

These reports help revenue teams compare campaign performance and make more informed budget decisions. Teams should still check how they record campaign costs, associate contacts with deals, and calculate attribution before using the results to evaluate marketing returns.

Sales and marketing teams manage different stages of the buyer journey, but they need shared definitions of target customers, qualified leads, and sales readiness. When those definitions differ, teams may contact prospects at the wrong time, overlook relevant engagement signals, or disagree about which opportunities belong in the pipeline.
A shared B2B buyer journey map can help teams identify the actions and information buyers need at each stage, along with the department responsible for the next step.

Marketing may keep sending leads that sales doesn’t consider ready, while sales may miss valuable context about what a prospect has already viewed, downloaded, or responded to. Over time, that can lead to wasted spend, slower follow-up, and more friction around who’s responsible for pipeline performance.
How to Diagnose Sales and Marketing Misalignment
Sales regularly rejecting leads that marketing considers qualified.
Both teams using different definitions for lifecycle stages or lead quality.
The marketing team losing visibility once a lead is handed to sales.
Sales reps can’t see which campaigns or content influenced a prospect.
Pipeline or revenue numbers differing between teams.
Lead handoffs relying heavily on manual updates.

Data Hub helps teams standardize and synchronize customer information across connected systems. This can reduce conflicting account records and give sales and marketing teams a more consistent foundation for their shared workflows.

Marketing Hub’s lead scoring tools can help teams prioritize prospects based on defined fit and engagement criteria. Marketing and sales leaders still need to agree on those criteria and determine what should trigger a handoff.

When teams use Data Hub alongside Marketing Hub and Sales Hub, they can build workflows that share relevant engagement signals, assign follow-up responsibilities, and incorporate sales outcomes into marketing reporting. B2B marketing automation can also help teams nurture prospects until they meet agreed qualification criteria.
To measure whether those changes work, teams should track lead acceptance, time to follow-up, and conversion rates between agreed lifecycle stages.
Lead Generation Challenges for Complex B2B Audiences

Lead generation gets more complicated when a business isn’t selling to one person, but to an entire buying group. An enterprise software purchase, for example, might involve a department head, IT, finance, procurement, and several end users, all with different priorities and varying levels of influence over the decision.

Generating interest from one contact does not necessarily mean the broader buying group is ready to purchase. Revenue teams need to identify relevant accounts, understand which stakeholders influence the purchase, and tailor their communications to each person’s priorities.

Account-based marketing can help coordinate that effort across decision-makers. HubSpot’s account-based marketing statistics provide additional background on this approach, although teams should use their own current data to assess lead quality and account engagement.
How to Diagnose Lead Generation Problems Within Complex Audiences
This challenge may show up when:
Marketing generates plenty of leads, but only a few turn into qualified opportunities.
Reps engage one contact without knowing who else influences the purchase.
Teams struggle to identify which accounts to prioritize.
Outreach looks the same across accounts with very different needs.
High-value accounts show engagement, but sales and marketing don’t coordinate follow-up across the buying group.

HubSpot’s account-based marketing (ABM) software helps teams organize lead generation around target accounts instead of individual contacts. Its ABM features are available with Marketing Hub Professional, Marketing Hub Enterprise, Sales Hub Professional, or Sales Hub Enterprise, with seat requirements for some features.

Once those accounts are selected, marketers and sales reps can track key contacts, engagement across the account, open deals, and deal value from one workspace. That makes it easier to coordinate outreach across the full buying group and tailor campaigns to each account’s needs and activity.
Difficulty Maintaining a Consistent Customer Experience

A consistent customer experience helps customers receive relevant information and support across channels and departments. For B2B companies, that becomes harder when support requests are spread across inboxes, account histories are incomplete, or response times depend on which employee receives the request.
A coordinated B2B customer experience requires teams to share relevant account information, set response standards, and clarify responsibilities.

Inconsistency can show up in small but frustrating ways, like customers having to repeat information they’ve already shared, urgent requests taking too long to reach the right person, or support teams responding without the full account history.
How to Diagnose an Inconsistent Customer Experience
Common warning signs of this include:
Customers regularly repeating the same information to different teams.
Response times varying widely by channel or rep.
Support requests getting lost or sitting unassigned.
Reps having to search other systems for account history.
High-priority customers not receiving fast support when they request it.

Service Hub helps support teams manage customer requests through a connected help desk workspace. Depending on the subscription and channel configuration, teams can bring email, chat, Facebook Messenger, WhatsApp, and other supported conversations into the workspace.

Service Hub Professional and Enterprise support automatic ticket routing, while advanced skill-based routing requires Service Hub Enterprise. Teams can also configure ticket assignment according to availability, workload, and other supported routing criteria.

Because help desk tickets connect to CRM records, authorized support employees can review available customer information, previous interactions, and related account activity without searching multiple disconnected systems.

Service Hub also supports service-level agreement (SLA) goals that help teams track response and resolution times. For example, a support team can configure a two-hour first-response goal for high-priority tickets and monitor when requests approach or exceed that threshold. Additional automation can support escalations when the account’s subscription and workflow configuration allow it.

B2B pricing can get complicated fast, especially when deals involve custom packages, volume discounts, multiple contract terms, or usage-based pricing. Reps may need to adjust quotes for different account sizes, regions, products, or renewal structures while still staying within approved pricing rules.

That leaves room for mistakes. A rep might apply the wrong discount, use an outdated price sheet, or build a quote that finance later has to correct. Those delays can slow negotiations and make the buying process harder than it needs to be.
Pricing may be creating friction if:
Reps build quotes manually in spreadsheets or separate tools.
Discount approvals require several back-and-forth messages.
Pricing rules vary widely by account or contract type.
Quotes are frequently revised because of errors or missing approvals.
Sales and finance teams use different pricing information.
Complex deals take much longer to price than standard ones.

Depending on their subscription, teams can use tiered pricing, approved price books, quote templates, and pricing rules to reduce manual quote preparation.

For complex deals, HubSpot CPQ supports configurations such as tiered pricing, multi-year pricing changes, and recurring or usage-based charges. Businesses can establish approved products and pricing structures, then use the quote-building and approval features available in their Revenue Hub subscription.

Revenue Hub Enterprise includes advanced quote approvals and quote rules. These controls help teams review exceptions before sending quotes, but the organization still needs accurate product information, pricing policies, and clear approval responsibilities.

The risk with manual processes is that important tasks only happen when someone remembers to do them. If someone forgets to update a spreadsheet, pass information to another team, or route a lead to the right rep, the process breaks down, and the information everyone else relies on quickly becomes incomplete or outdated.

There’s also key-person risk. If one employee is the only person who knows how a process works, progress can stall when they’re unavailable or leave the company. Documented playbooks, standardized handoffs, and automation help turn that individual knowledge into a process the wider team can follow.
How to Diagnose Overreliance on Manual Processes
Important workflows depend on spreadsheets, reminders, or manual data entry.
Only one or two employees know how certain processes work.
Leads or customers get handled differently depending on the rep.
Handoffs regularly require someone to chase another team for an update.
Routine CRM maintenance takes up a noticeable part of the team’s week.
Workflows stop or require extra intervention when a key employee is unavailable.

Data Hub helps teams reduce manual work through data synchronization, quality controls, and automation. Its programmable automation capabilities can support custom data-processing tasks that standard workflows cannot handle.

Data synchronization: Data Hub can synchronize supported records between HubSpot and connected applications. For example, the QuickBooks Online integration can keep selected customer, product, invoice, and payment information synchronized according to the integration’s settings.

Data quality: Data Hub’s data quality tools can identify duplicate records and formatting problems. Eligible subscriptions also support automated formatting rules that help prevent recurring data-entry errors.

The goal isn’t to automate every revenue process, but to reduce repetitive work while giving teams documented rules, clear responsibilities, and reliable information. Businesses still need to review their workflows and confirm that automated decisions produce the intended results.

Customization can help win complex B2B deals, but too much bespoke work comes with a cost. If every customer gets a different package, workflow, implementation plan, or set of terms, sales and delivery teams have to spend more time figuring out how each deal should work.

That can extend timelines, make the customer experience less consistent, and eat into margins as more hours go into work that can’t easily be reused. A better approach is to standardize the core offer, then give customers a defined set of modules or add-ons they can combine as needed.
How to Tell When Customization Has Gone Too Far
Similar customers regularly receive very different packages.
Reps need internal help to structure most proposals.
Delivery teams frequently have to interpret what sales promised.
Custom work adds significant time before onboarding can begin.
Margins vary widely between otherwise similar deals.
Teams rebuild successful solutions from scratch instead of reusing them.

Revenue Hub helps teams standardize quoting and revenue processes. Its CPQ tools include a product library where businesses can define products and services, establish supported pricing models, and use those records when preparing deals and quotes.

Teams can establish standard packages and add approved products or services to meet a buyer’s requirements instead of rebuilding every proposal from scratch. Quote templates can help sales reps present these options consistently, while pricing rules and advanced approval workflows in eligible Revenue Hub subscriptions can help businesses control exceptions.
A consistent product catalog can reduce repeated setup work. However, sales and delivery teams still need to agree on what each package includes and when a custom request requires additional review.
What about B2B manufacturing and other complex industries?

B2B manufacturing illustrates how long sales cycles, complicated buyer requirements, and multiple business relationships can create revenue challenges. A manufacturer may sell through distributors, negotiate large contracts, and need technical or compliance approvals before a buyer commits.

Consider a manufacturer selling specialized equipment through channel partners. The sales team may need to track distributors, end customers, product specifications, pricing approvals, and expected delivery dates. If those details live in separate systems, employees can lose time reconciling information or correcting inconsistent quotes.
The complexity continues after the sale. Customer relationships may span years and involve service agreements, replacement parts, repeat orders, and ongoing distributor relationships.

For businesses with these requirements, the right technology must do more than store contact records. Teams need connected account information, visibility into lengthy buying cycles, reliable pricing and approval workflows, and a way to share relevant information across sales, service, and operations.

Manufacturing is one example. Other B2B industries with large buying groups, multiple channel partners, or long-term customer relationships may face similar challenges. The appropriate technology depends on the company’s operating requirements and the systems it needs to connect.
How to Evaluate a Unified Customer Platform

Before choosing a unified customer platform, revenue and IT leaders should identify the problems they need to solve and the systems they need to retain. A platform that consolidates customer data can reduce duplicated work, but consolidation is not automatically the right solution for every organization.
Use the following criteria to evaluate the options.

Data unification: Can the platform connect customer information across marketing, sales, service, and other relevant systems? Check which records and fields can sync, how frequently updates occur, and whether users can identify conflicting or duplicate information.

Governance and security: Can administrators control who accesses, creates, and changes customer information? Evaluate permissions, data quality controls, audit capabilities, security documentation, and the organization’s privacy and compliance requirements.

AI readiness: Does the platform provide the data quality, governance, and approved integrations needed for responsible AI use? Assess which information AI tools can access, what data they transmit or retain, whether the organization has the necessary permissions and consent, and where employees must review AI-generated outputs or decisions. Test limitations and errors before expanding AI use to customer-facing or sensitive processes.

Automation: Which tasks can teams automate without losing necessary oversight? Prioritize repetitive work such as data updates, lead assignment, and handoffs. Confirm how the system handles exceptions, failed workflows, and situations that require employee approval.

Total cost of ownership: What will the platform cost beyond its subscription price? Include required user seats, implementation and onboarding, data migration, integrations, training, ongoing administration, and any usage-based charges. Compare those expenses with the cost of maintaining the existing systems.

Time to value: How soon can the organization begin using the platform to address its priority problems? Evaluate migration requirements, implementation resources, employee training, and the time needed to establish reliable reporting. A phased rollout with measurable goals can help teams evaluate progress before expanding.

Ecosystem fit: How well does the platform work with the applications the business plans to retain? Confirm that supported integrations handle the required records and workflows, and determine how much custom development or maintenance they will require.

Before committing, teams should define the outcomes that would justify a change. For example, they might aim to reduce manual data reconciliation, shorten the time between lead qualification and sales follow-up, or make pipeline reporting more consistent across departments.
